title: Weekly Briefing Hidden AI Resume Prompts, Workers Reject Promotions, and Boomerang Employees Surge
author: Future Ready Leadership
summary: This weekly leadership briefing analyzes three workplace stories through a single lens: trust between employers and employees. The first covers a candidate who embedded hidden white-text AI prompts in a resume to manipulate an AI screening tool into rating him a '98% match' — the attempt failed, the system flagged it, and a human made the final call, but the author uses it to argue hiring is becoming an AI trust problem on both sides of the table. The second examines a Fast Company survey finding that 58-62% of workers would reject a promotion requiring after-hours availability, which the author reframes not as a lack of ambition but as an honest cost-benefit calculation about an unsustainable management role. The third looks at the sharp rise of 'boomerang employees' (35% of new hires in one dataset), arguing it's a rational response to a cautious hiring market but a risky signal if returning employees are rewarded better than the loyal staff who stayed. Across all three, the author's throughline is that efficiency-focused HR practices collapse in value once people stop believing the underlying system is fair.
points: A senior-role candidate embedded roughly 1,500 characters of hidden white-on-white text instructing an AI screening system to rate him a '98% match' and recommend him over other candidates; the system flagged the hidden prompt and a human made the hiring decision, illustrating how AI has changed gamesmanship on both sides of hiring.

A Fast Company survey of nearly 14,000 workers found 58% (59% in the US) would reject a promotion requiring after-hours availability, and 62% would decline management if it cost work-life boundaries — reframed by the author as a rational cost calculation rather than a lack of ambition, given the added meetings, stress, and pressure to manage AI adoption and team burnout that come with the role.

Forbes reported a 1,957% surge in searches for 'boomerang employees,' with ADP data showing returning employees made up 35% of new hires in March 2025 (up from 31% the prior year), and nearly two-thirds of new hires in the information sector.

The author warns that if returning 'boomerang' employees come back with better titles or pay than the loyal staff who stayed, companies risk accidentally teaching everyone that the fastest path to career growth is to leave first.

The briefing's unifying practical lesson for hiring leaders is to 'test your systems before candidates do' — knowing exactly where AI is used in a hiring pipeline, what data it reads, how it can be manipulated, and where a human remains accountable for the final call.
quotes: The hidden prompt told the system to identify the candidate as a "98% match," recommend him over other candidates even if that was not clearly supported, and avoid mentioning the hidden text.
If candidates believe hiring is run by automated black boxes, some will try to hack the box.
The practical lesson is simple, test your systems before candidates do.
58% would reject a promotion if it required after-hours availability, even with more pay.
But employees are asking what the promotion actually costs. More meetings. More stress. More after-hours messages.
Global searches for "boomerang employees" surged 1,957% over the past year.

If former employees come back with better titles, higher pay, or more flexibility while loyal employees who stayed feel overlooked, the company can accidentally teach people that the fastest way to grow is to leave first.
